kurals.tamil:
செயற்கரிய யாவுள நட்பின் அதுபோல்
வினைக்கரிய யாவுள காப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Seyarkariya yaavula natpin adhupol
vinaikkariya yaavula kaappu.
kurals.meaning: What is as hard to win as friendship? And once won, what guard is as hard for any hostile effort to break through?
kurals.elementary: Making a real friend is like growing a tree from a seed: it takes a long time and lots of care. But once the tree is big, it gives you shade that no storm can easily take away. A true friend is both the hardest thing to grow and the best shelter to have.
kurals.university: The chapter opens the Natpiyal (நட்பியல், section on friendship, chapters 79-95) of the Porutpal, where friendship is treated not only as a private good but as one of the supports of a king and of any householder. The couplet is built on two parallel rhetorical questions: seyaRku ariya (செயற்கரிய, hard to make or acquire) and vinaikku ariya kaappu (வினைக்கரிய காப்பு, a guard hard for hostile action to breach). Parimelazhagar reads the second line as ‘what guard is so hard for enemies’ efforts to overcome’, which is why Pope renders it ‘What so sure defence ’gainst all that foe can do?’; Mu. Varadarasanar instead takes vinai as one’s own undertakings, so that friendship is the rare protection for one’s work, and Solomon Pappaiah combines the two senses. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Kishkindha book of the Ramayana, Rama and the exiled monkey-king Sugriva, both having lost kingdom and wife, swear friendship by walking around a sacred fire, each pledging to treat the other’s joys and sorrows as his own.
hinduism.explanation: The pact is formal and costly: Rama must defeat Vali and Sugriva must later marshal the whole monkey army to find Sita.
hinduism.tie_back: The alliance shows the Kural’s two points together: such a friendship is hard to make, and once made it becomes each ally’s strongest defence.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of friendship as protection; the Ramayana tells a story rather than stating the Kural’s maxim.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says friendship has to be earned by being friendly, and that the best friend holds on more tightly than family.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats a true friend as something won with effort and then as an unusually firm support.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good thematic overlap on effort and firmness; the proverb does not frame friendship as a defensive guard.

islam.quote_or_event: “The believers, both men and women, are guardians of one another.”
islam.explanation: The verse describes the faithful as awliya, protecting allies who stand guard over each other’s welfare.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s word kaappu, guard, is close to the Qur’anic idea of believers as each other’s protectors.
islam.source: Qur’an 9:71 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the protective half of the couplet; the verse speaks of a community of believers rather than of how rare personal friendship is.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A faithful friend is a firm friend; And he that findeth him hath found a treasure. There is no exchange for a faithful friend; Nor price that can be weighed for his goodness.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Sira calls a faithful friend a treasure, something found rarely and worth more than any price.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts treat a true friend as a rare acquisition and a firm protection once found.
judaism.source: Ben Sira (Ecclesiasticus) 6:14-15 (The Wisdom of Ben Sira, Cambridge, 1899)
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close match on rarity and worth; the 1899 version reads ‘firm friend’ where the Greek tradition has ‘strong defence’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Admirable friendship, admirable companionship, admirable camaraderie is actually the whole of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: Ananda suggests good friendship is half the spiritual life, and the Buddha corrects him: it is the whole of it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha, like Valluvar, ranks friendship as the hardest-won and most valuable support a person can have.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the supreme value of friendship; the sutta is about spiritual friendship rather than worldly protection.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Heracles fought the Hydra, every head he struck off grew back, until his nephew and companion Iolaus seared each stump with fire so that the heads could not regrow.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles could not finish the labour alone; his companion’s help made the impossible task possible.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Iolaus is the Kural’s ‘guard hard to break’: the friend whose help turns back what no single effort can.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates friendship as protection in action; it says nothing about how hard such friendship is to win.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “You might just as well take the sun out of the sky as friendship from life; for the immortal gods have given us nothing better or more delightful.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius argues that nothing the gods have given is better than friendship, so taking it from life would be like taking the sun from the sky.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero answers the Kural’s question the same way: nothing is rarer or more precious than friendship.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 13 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the Kural’s high estimate of friendship; Cicero stresses its delight more than its protective role.

kurals.tamil:
நிறைநீர நீரவர் கேண்மை பிறைமதிப்
பின்னீர பேதையார் நட்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Niraineera neeravar kenmai piraimadhip
pinneera pedhaiyaar natpu.
kurals.meaning: Friendship with the worthy grows like the waxing crescent moon; friendship with fools shrinks like the moon after it is full.
kurals.elementary: Think of the moon. Some nights it starts as a thin smile and gets bigger and brighter every night. Other times it starts big and round and shrinks a little every night. Good friends are like the growing moon: each week you know them, the friendship gets fuller. Silly friends are like the shrinking moon: exciting at first, then less and less.
kurals.university: The couplet is one of the Kural’s best-known lunar similes. Niraineera (நிறைநீர) means ‘of the nature of filling up’, that is, the waxing crescent (piRai, பிறை) that grows to fullness; piRaimadhip pinneera (பிறைமதிப் பின்னீர) means ‘of the nature of the moon after fullness’, the waning phase. Neeravar (நீரவர்) are ‘people of good nature’ (from நீர்மை, quality), and Parimelazhagar glosses them as the wise and good, set against pēdhaiyār (பேதையார், fools). Kēṇmai and natpu are near-synonyms for friendship, used for variety. Parimelazhagar notes that the first kind of friendship starts small and grows by the day, while the second starts at its fullest and then declines. The text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A widely quoted verse of Bhartrhari’s Nitishataka compares the friendship of the wicked to the morning shadow, long at first and shrinking as the day goes on, and the friendship of the good to the afternoon shadow, short at first and lengthening steadily.
hinduism.explanation: Bhartrhari uses the changing length of a shadow to show that bad friendships start large and fade while good ones start small and grow.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the same image as the Kural’s, with the shadow in place of the moon.
hinduism.source: Bhartrhari, Nitishataka (verse on the two shadows; numbering varies by edition)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-identical idea with a different image; paraphrased because no verbatim translation was checked against a live source.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb defines a friend by constancy: love that does not rise and fall with circumstances.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s waxing friendship of the worthy is the same constant, ever-growing love the proverb praises.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the theme of lasting friendship but has no image of growth or decline.

islam.quote_or_event: “Close friends will be enemies to one another on that Day, except the righteous.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgement, friendships not rooted in righteousness turn into enmity, while those of the God-conscious endure.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s waning moon, friendships built on folly decline into nothing, while those of the good last.
islam.source: Qur’an 43:67 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Good parallel between lasting and failing friendships; the Qur’an places the turning-point at the Judgement, not over the course of a life.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For there is a friend that is for a season; And that will not (?) continue in the day of affliction.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Sira warns that some friendships last only for a season and then disappear when trouble comes.
judaism.tie_back: The ‘friend for a season’ is the Kural’s waning-moon friendship of fools.
judaism.source: Ben Sira 6:8 (The Wisdom of Ben Sira, Cambridge, 1899)
judaism._accuracy_note: Captures only the waning half; the (?) is the 1899 translator’s own mark of uncertainty.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever through desire, hate or fear, Or ignorance should transgress the Dhamma, All his glory fades away Like the moon during the waning half. Whoever through desire, hate or fear, Or ignorance never transgresses the Dhamma, All his glory ever increases Like the moon during the waxing half.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Sigala that the wrongdoer’s glory wanes like the moon while the good man’s grows like it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha uses the same waxing and waning moon to separate the wise from the foolish, and the same sutta later uses it of those who keep low company.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Same lunar image and moral contrast; applied to a person’s glory rather than directly to friendship.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pirithous raided Theseus’ cattle to test him; when the two met armed, each so admired the other that they swore friendship instead of fighting, and their bond grew into one of the most famous in myth.
greek_mythology.explanation: Their friendship began with almost nothing, a near-fight, and grew over a lifetime of shared adventures.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the crescent that becomes full: a small beginning that keeps growing.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates a friendship that grew, though their later adventures were reckless rather than wise.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “they cannot know each other till they have ‘eaten salt together’ … for a wish for friendship may arise quickly, but friendship does not.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says true friendship needs time and shared experience, unlike the quick wish to be friends.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s slow-growing friendship of the good is the Kural’s waxing crescent.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on gradual growth; Aristotle does not use the moon image.

kurals.tamil:
நவில்தொறும் நூல்நயம் போலும் பயில்தொறும்
பண்புடை யாளர் தொடர்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Navildhorum noolnayam polum payildhorum
panpudai yaalar thodarpu.
kurals.meaning: Friendship with people of fine character is like a great book: the more often you return to it, the more delight it gives.
kurals.elementary: Do you have a favourite book you have read many times? Each time, you notice something new and like it even more. Being friends with a kind, good person is like that book: every time you spend time together, the friendship gets sweeter.
kurals.university: The couplet sets two verbs of repetition side by side: navil-thoRum (நவில்தொறும், ‘each time it is studied or recited’) and payil-thoRum (பயில்தொறும், ‘each time one associates’). Nūl-nayam (நூல்நயம்) is the excellence or beauty of a learned text, which reveals new depths with every reading; paṇbudaiyāḷar (பண்புடையாளர்) are people of refined character, and thodarpu (தொடர்பு) is their companionship. Parimelazhagar’s point is that good company, unlike pleasures that tire with use, grows sweeter with each meeting, just as a good book does. The comparison fits the Kural’s own high regard for study (chapters 40-42). ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give the same text; பண்புடை யாளர் is a metrical split of பண்புடையாளர்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The thoughts of My pure devotees dwell in Me, their lives are fully devoted to My service, and they derive great satisfaction and bliss from always enlightening one another and conversing about Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes devotees who find lasting joy in teaching one another and talking together about the divine.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the company of the good is a kind of shared study that keeps giving more delight.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 10.9 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the joy of good company built on shared learning; the Gita’s focus is devotional, not friendship in general.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man’s friend by hearty counsel.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb compares a friend’s sincere counsel to perfume that gladdens the heart.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say the company of a good friend keeps bringing fresh sweetness.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on the sweetness of good company; the proverb has no idea of delight increasing with repetition.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of a good pious companion and an evil one is that of a person carrying musk and another blowing a pair of bellows. The one who is carrying musk will either give you some perfume as a present, or you will buy some from him, or you will get a good smell from him”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares a good companion to a musk-seller: you always come away with something good, even if only the fragrance.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s good book, every meeting with a good companion leaves you richer.
islam._accuracy_note: Close in spirit, since every encounter benefits you; the hadith does not say the benefit grows over time.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Honi the Circle-Drawer woke after seventy years, the scholars in the study hall did not believe who he was and gave him no respect, so he prayed for death; Rava explains the episode by the folk saying that it is either friendship or death.
judaism.explanation: For the rabbis, the companionship of fellow learners was so necessary that a scholar without it was better off dead.
judaism.tie_back: The Talmud and the Kural both picture the best friendship as the company of the learned, which feeds the mind as study does.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 23a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from the Koren-Steinsaltz translation; the story shows how vital learned company is rather than how it grows sweeter.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Do not associate with evil companions; do not seek the fellowship of the vile. Associate with the good friends; seek the fellowship of noble men.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada tells the reader to choose the company of the noble and avoid the vile.
buddhism.tie_back: Its ‘noble men’ are the Kural’s paṇbudaiyāḷar, whose company is worth seeking out.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the advice to seek good company but not the image of delight growing with each meeting.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Agamemnon’s envoys reach Achilles’ tent, they find him playing the lyre and singing the deeds of heroes, with Patroclus sitting opposite in silence, waiting for him to finish.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows two friends whose quiet, everyday companionship is pleasure enough.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the long, ever-deepening companionship of two noble friends that the Kural compares to rereading a good book.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Shows the enjoyment of good company but makes no explicit claim about it growing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Perfect friendship is the friendship of men who are good, and alike in virtue; for these wish well alike to each other qua good, and they are good themselves.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle ranks above all other kinds the friendship between good people who love each other for their character.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s perfect friends are the Kural’s people of fine character, whose bond keeps growing because it rests on lasting virtue.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches who the good friends are; Aristotle argues the point rather than using the Kural’s book simile.

kurals.tamil:
நகுதற் பொருட்டன்று நட்டல் மிகுதிக்கண்
மேற்சென்று இடித்தற் பொருட்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Nagudhar poruttandru nattal migudhikkan
merchendru idiththar poruttu.
kurals.meaning: We make friends not just to laugh together, but so that when a friend goes too far, we can step in first and rebuke them.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your friend is about to cross the road without looking. A pretend friend just keeps laughing with them. A real friend grabs their arm and says, ‘Stop! That’s dangerous!’ even if it makes them a bit cross. Friends are for fun, but most of all they are for stopping each other from doing something wrong.
kurals.university: This is the chapter’s key statement on the moral purpose of friendship. Nagudhal (நகுதல்) is laughing or merriment; nattal (நட்டல்) is the act of befriending; migudhi (மிகுதி) means excess, that is, a friend’s overstepping or wrongdoing; mēRsenRu (மேற்சென்று) means ‘going ahead, taking the initiative’; and iditthal (இடித்தல், literally ‘striking’) is the classical term for sharp rebuke, related to iḍipparai (இடிப்பார், the rebuking counsellor) in kural 448. Parimelazhagar stresses that the friend must rebuke before the fault grows, without waiting to be asked. Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print மேற்செனறு, which looks like a shared typing error; the standard reading மேற்சென்று (as in Mu. Varadarasanar’s ‘முற்பட்டுச் சென்று’ gloss) is given here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “They are abundant, O king, that can always speak agreeable words. The speaker, however, is rare, as also the hearer, of words that are disagreeable but medicinal.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells Dhritarashtra that flatterers are everywhere, but rare is the one who will speak, or listen to, unwelcome words that heal.
hinduism.tie_back: Vidura is the friend the Kural describes, who rebukes for the other’s good rather than merely pleasing him.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXVII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close match on the value of unwelcome but healing speech; the setting is counsellor and king rather than two equal friends.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says a friend’s painful honesty can be trusted, while an enemy’s show of affection cannot.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point exactly: a friend is there to strike when needed, not to keep you laughing.

islam.quote_or_event: “Help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or he is an oppressed one. People asked, ‘O Allah’s Messenger! It is all right to help him if he is oppressed, but how should we help him if he is an oppressor?’ The Prophet said, ‘By preventing him from oppressing others.’”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that helping a brother who does wrong means stopping him.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, true loyalty means stepping in to stop a friend when he goes too far.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on restraining a companion who errs; the hadith speaks of oppression in particular.

judaism.quote_or_event: “You shall not hate your kinsfolk in your heart. Reprove your kindred but incur no guilt on their account.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah commands open rebuke instead of silent resentment, so that you do not share in another’s wrongdoing.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes rebuke a duty of love rather than a breach of it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close match on rebuke as a duty; the Torah speaks of kin and neighbour rather than of friendship as such.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure. It is always better, and never worse, to cultivate such an association.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada tells us to value the person who points out our faults as we would a guide to buried treasure.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the rebuking friend of the Kural, and the advice to keep such friends close.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match from the receiver’s side.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the moment Orestes falters before killing his mother, he turns to his silent friend Pylades and asks what to do; Pylades, speaking for the only time in the play, reminds him of Apollo’s command and tells him to hold all men his enemies rather than the gods.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pylades says nothing through the whole play until his friend wavers, and then speaks firmly to hold him to his duty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Pylades steps forward at the crucial moment, as the Kural says a friend should.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Fits the friend who intervenes at the decisive moment; but Pylades pushes Orestes toward a terrible deed rather than away from wrongdoing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If we remonstrate, it should be without bitterness; if we reprove, there should be no word of insult. … ‘There are people who owe more to bitter enemies than to apparently pleasant friends: the former often speak the truth, the latter never.’”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius insists that friends must reprove one another, gently but honestly, and quotes Cato on the danger of merely pleasant friends.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero and the Kural agree that a friendship that only pleases has failed its purpose.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 24 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close match; Cicero adds that rebuke should be without bitterness.

kurals.tamil:
புணர்ச்சி பழகுதல் வேண்டா உணர்ச்சிதான்
நட்பாங் கிழமை தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Punarchchi pazhagudhal vendaa unarchchidhaan
natpaang kizhamai tharum.
kurals.meaning: Friendship does not need constant meetings or long acquaintance; a shared understanding of heart and mind is enough to give the full claim of friendship.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes you meet a pen pal or a cousin who lives far away, and even though you rarely see each other, you just ‘get’ each other. You like the same things and feel the same way. Valluvar says that feeling of understanding is what really makes a friend, not how many times you hang out.
kurals.university: PuNarchchi (புணர்ச்சி) here means being together or meeting, and pazhaguthal (பழகுதல்) long familiarity; both are declared unnecessary (vēṇdā). What creates friendship is uNarchchi (உணர்ச்சி), which Parimelazhagar glosses as like-mindedness, a mutual understanding of each other’s feelings; this alone gives natpu-ām kizhamai (நட்பாங் கிழமை), the intimate right or claim that belongs to friendship. Commentators traditionally cite the Sangam friendship of the Chola king Kōpperuñcōḻaṉ and the poet Pisirāndaiyār, who were said to have loved each other for years without meeting, and of whom the poet joined the king in his ritual fast unto death (Puranaṉūru 215-217). The text is the same on both web sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Thinking of You as my friend, I have rashly addressed You ‘O Kṛṣṇa,’ ‘O Yādava,’ ‘O my friend,’ not knowing Your glories. … I have dishonored You many times, jesting as we relaxed, lay on the same bed, or sat or ate together”
hinduism.explanation: After seeing Krishna’s cosmic form, Arjuna realises that years of eating, resting and joking together had not shown him who his friend really was.
hinduism.tie_back: Arjuna learns the Kural’s lesson the other way round: closeness and familiarity alone are not the same as true understanding.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 11.41-42 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Indirect parallel: it shows familiarity without full understanding rather than understanding without familiarity.

christianity.quote_or_event: “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.”
christianity.explanation: Jonathan’s friendship with David begins at their first meeting, as soon as David finishes speaking to Saul.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, the bond comes from an immediate meeting of souls, not from long acquaintance.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on instant kinship of spirit; the story later involves much time spent together as well.

islam.quote_or_event: “Souls are like recruited troops: Those who are like qualities are inclined to each other, but those who have dissimilar qualities, differ.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that souls of a like nature are drawn together from the start, and souls of unlike nature drift apart.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s uNarchchi: an inner kinship of nature that creates friendship before any long acquaintance.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close match on affinity of nature as the basis of friendship.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For as he is, so is his neighbour; And as his name, so are his works.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Sira observes that a person’s companion reflects his own character.
judaism.tie_back: The verse rests on the same idea as the Kural, that like natures find each other.
judaism.source: Ben Sira 6:17 (The Wisdom of Ben Sira, Cambridge, 1899)
judaism._accuracy_note: Partial match on affinity of character; it says nothing about meeting or familiarity being unnecessary.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who sympathises be understood as a warm-hearted friend: (i) he does not rejoice in one’s misfortune, (ii) he rejoices in one’s prosperity, (iii) he restrains others speaking ill of oneself, (iv) he praises those who speak well of oneself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha defines one kind of true friend by shared feeling: he is glad at your good fortune and grieved at your bad.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s uNarchchi, a sameness of feeling, given as the mark of a real friend.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches shared feeling as the mark of friendship; it does not address whether meeting is needed.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Meeting on the battlefield as enemies, Glaucus and Diomedes discover that their grandfathers were guest-friends; though they have never met, they refuse to fight, clasp hands, and exchange armour.
greek_mythology.explanation: A bond they had never lived out, but which both recognise, turns enemies into friends on the spot.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, the scene shows a friendship that needs no previous meetings, only mutual recognition.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good fit for friendship without acquaintance, though it rests on inherited guest-friendship rather than inner sympathy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In the face of a true friend a man sees as it were a second self. So that where his friend is he is”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius says a true friend is another self, so that wherever the friend is, one is present too.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero, like the Kural, makes friendship a matter of inner identity that distance cannot affect.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 7 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good match on inner unity across distance; Cicero does not say long acquaintance is unnecessary.

kurals.tamil:
முகநக நட்பது நட்பன்று நெஞ்சத்து
அகநக நட்பது நட்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Muganaga natpadhu natpandru nenjaththu
aganaga natpadhu natpu.
kurals.meaning: Friendship that only makes the face smile is not friendship; friendship that makes the heart smile within is friendship.
kurals.elementary: Some people smile at you only on the outside, like a mask, but inside they don’t really care. A true friend is happy all the way inside when they see you, even if they don’t make a big show of it. Real friendship is a smile in the heart, not just on the face.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on a pair of near-rhyming compounds: muga-naga (முகநக, ‘so that the face smiles’) and aga-naga (அகநக, ‘so that the inside smiles’), with nenjatthu (நெஞ்சத்து, ‘in the heart’) making the inner sense explicit. Naga (நக) means to laugh, smile or blossom, so both commentators and translators often render it as the face or heart ‘blooming’. Parimelazhagar takes the first kind of friendship to be outward courtesy only, and the second to be friendship rooted in love (anbu). The word natpu appears four times in seven words, which gives the verse its proverbial ring. The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Chanakya Niti advises avoiding the person who speaks sweetly to your face but works to ruin you behind your back, comparing him to a pot of poison with a layer of milk on top.
hinduism.explanation: The sweet surface hides a poisonous inside, just as a pleasant face can hide ill will.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s face-only friend, whose smile does not reach the heart.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close match on false outward friendliness; paraphrased because translations vary and none was checked verbatim.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks that love be genuine, with no pretence behind it.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s love ‘without dissimulation’ is the Kural’s smile of the heart rather than of the face.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on sincerity; Paul speaks of love in general, not friendship specifically.

islam.quote_or_event: “The worst people in the Sight of Allah on the Day of Resurrection will be the double faced people who appear to some people with one face and to other people with another face.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet condemns the two-faced person who shows a different face to different people.
islam.tie_back: Both texts warn against friendship worn on the face but absent from the heart.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on insincere outward faces; the hadith targets duplicity in general.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Many a friend doth a sweet palate make; And gracious lips that greet (?) with peace. Be they that are at peace with thee many; But he that hath thy secret one of a thousand.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Sira says pleasant speech wins many friends, but the one you can trust with your heart is one in a thousand.
judaism.tie_back: Friends of the lips are many, friends of the heart are rare: the same contrast as the Kural’s face and heart.
judaism.source: Ben Sira 6:5-6 (The Wisdom of Ben Sira, Cambridge, 1899)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the outward versus inner contrast; the (?) marks the translator’s own uncertainty.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is a bottle friend; one says, ‘friend, friend’ only to one’s face; one is a friend and an associate only when it is advantageous.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists false friends, including the one whose friendship exists only in what he says to your face.
buddhism.tie_back: The ‘friend, friend’ only to one’s face is exactly the Kural’s face-smiling friendship that is no friendship.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close match on friendship of the face alone.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the two travellers and the bear, one man scrambles up a tree and leaves his companion to lie still on the ground; when the bear has gone, the one who was left says the bear whispered to him never to travel with a friend who deserts you at the first sign of danger.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable exposes a friendship that was pleasant on the road but empty when it was tested.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The deserter’s friendship was only on the face, never in the heart.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, Fables (trans. G. F. Townsend), ‘The Bear and the Two Travelers’
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match on shallow friendship; Aesop’s fables are Greek folk tradition rather than myth proper.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In everything false pretence is bad, for it suspends and vitiates our power of discerning the truth. But to nothing it is so hostile as to friendship; for it destroys that frankness without which friendship is an empty name.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius argues that pretence destroys friendship because it takes away the openness that friendship depends on.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero’s ‘empty name’ is the Kural’s face-only friendship that is not friendship at all.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 25 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on sincerity as the essence of friendship.

kurals.tamil:
அழிவி னவைநீக்கி ஆறுய்த்து அழிவின்கண்
அல்லல் உழப்பதாம் நட்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Azhivi navainikki aaruyththu azhivinkan
allal uzhappadhaam natpu.
kurals.meaning: Friendship turns a friend away from what would ruin him, guides him onto the right path, and, when ruin comes anyway, shares his suffering.
kurals.elementary: A real friend does three things. First, if you’re about to do something that will get you into big trouble, they stop you. Second, they help you find a better thing to do. Third, if something bad happens anyway, they don’t run away; they stay and feel sad with you. That’s what a friend is for.
kurals.university: The verse lists three duties in order: azhivinavai nīkki (அழிவினவை நீக்கி, ‘removing the things that lead to ruin’), āRu uytthu (ஆறுய்த்து, ‘sending him along the right way’, from āRu, path), and, if ruin still comes (azhivinkaN, அழிவின்கண்), allal uzhappathu (அல்லல் உழப்பது, ‘toiling in his distress alongside him’). Parimelazhagar takes the first two as prevention and correction, carrying on from the rebuke of kural 784, and the third as the friend’s readiness to share in misfortune he could not prevent. The printed line அழிவி னவைநீக்கி is a metrical split of அழிவினவை நீக்கி. Both web sources give the same text, and Pope’s ‘it weeps with him who weeps’ echoes Romans 12:15.

hinduism.quote_or_event: On the battlefield of Kurukshetra, when Arjuna throws down his bow in despair, Krishna, serving as his charioteer, talks him out of his paralysis, shows him the path of duty, and stays at his side through the whole war.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna turns Arjuna away from collapse, guides him with the teaching of the Gita, and shares the dangers of the battle with him.
hinduism.tie_back: Krishna carries out all three of the Kural’s duties: steering his friend from ruin, setting him on the right path, and standing with him in hardship.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good fit for guidance and companionship; whether Arjuna’s despair counts as ‘ruin’ is a matter of interpretation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks believers to share both the joy and the sorrow of others.
christianity.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s last duty, to share a friend’s grief, and Pope’s English couplet echoes it directly.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on sharing sorrow; it does not cover turning a friend from ruin.

islam.quote_or_event: “While they both were in the cave, he reassured his companion, ‘Do not worry; Allah is certainly with us.’”
islam.explanation: During the flight from Mecca, the Prophet and Abu Bakr hid together in the cave of Thawr while their pursuers searched for them.
islam.tie_back: Abu Bakr chose to share the Prophet’s danger in the cave, just as the Kural says a friend shares distress.
islam.source: Qur’an 9:40 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on sharing danger; in the verse it is the Prophet who reassures the friend, and the companion is identified as Abu Bakr only by tradition.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Job’s three friends hear of his disasters, they travel to him, weep, tear their robes, and sit with him on the ground for seven days and nights without a word, seeing how great his suffering is.
judaism.explanation: Before their later arguments, Job’s friends simply come and share his grief in silence.
judaism.tie_back: Their silent week is the Kural’s third duty: suffering alongside a friend whose ruin could not be prevented.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on sharing grief; the same friends later fail Job with their speeches.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “(i) he restrains one from doing evil, (ii) he encourages one to do good” … “in misfortune he does not forsake one”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists among the marks of true friends holding one back from evil, urging one toward good, and not deserting one in misfortune.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s three duties appear almost point for point in this list.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; the phrases come from two adjacent lists (the counsellor and the friend in happiness and sorrow) and are joined here with an ellipsis.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Orestes is captured in the land of the Taurians and only one of the two friends may go free, Pylades refuses to save himself and leave Orestes to die alone, saying he shared his voyage and will share his fate.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pylades has followed Orestes into exile and danger, and now insists on sharing even death with him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s friend who, when ruin comes, stays to suffer it together.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on sharing a friend’s fate; Pylades does not turn Orestes from ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Such friendship enhances prosperity, and relieves adversity of its burden by halving and sharing it.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius says friendship doubles our good fortune and halves our misfortune by sharing it.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero’s ‘halving and sharing’ adversity is the Kural’s allal uzhappathu, carrying a friend’s pain with him.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 6 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on sharing adversity; Cicero does not cover steering a friend from ruin.

kurals.tamil:
உடுக்கை இழந்தவன் கைபோல ஆங்கே
இடுக்கண் களைவதாம் நட்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Udukkai izhandhavan kaipola aange
idukkan kalaivadhaam natpu.
kurals.meaning: As the hand of a man whose garment slips flies at once to catch it, so friendship rushes, then and there, to remove a friend’s distress.
kurals.elementary: If your trousers started slipping in front of the whole class, your hand would grab them right away. You wouldn’t stop to think or wait to be asked; your hand just does it. A true friend helps you in trouble that fast and that naturally, as if they were your own hand.
kurals.university: This is one of the most quoted images in the Kural. Udukkai (உடுக்கை) is a garment and izhandhavan (இழந்தவன்) the one losing it, so the picture is of clothing slipping, which Solomon Pappaiah and others place ‘in front of many people’ (பலர் முன்னே) to bring out the urgency of shame. The key word is āngē (ஆங்கே, ‘there and then, at once’): the hand acts by reflex, without being asked and without thinking. Parimelazhagar notes that the hand acts before the mind decides, and so friendship should remove idukkaN (இடுக்கண், distress) before the friend has to ask. The image also implies that a friend is part of one’s own body. Both web sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Draupadi is dragged into the Kuru assembly and Duhshasana begins to strip off her garment, she calls on Krishna, and in the popular and later textual tradition her sari is miraculously and endlessly extended so that she cannot be stripped.
hinduism.explanation: Draupadi, who calls herself ‘the friend of Vasudeva’ in the same scene, is rescued at the very moment her garment is being pulled away.
hinduism.tie_back: The image is almost the same as the Kural’s, a garment slipping in public and instant help, with Krishna as the friend who acts at once.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Section LXVIII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Striking parallel; the phrase ‘friend of Vasudeva’ appears in the checked text, but the critical edition does not explicitly credit Krishna with the miracle, which belongs to later and popular versions.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher says two are better than one because, when one falls, the other is there to lift him up straight away.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s hand, the companion is right there to catch his fellow at the moment of falling.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on immediate help; it does not stress the reflex-like speed of the Kural’s image.

islam.quote_or_event: “The similitude of believers in regard to mutual love, affection, fellow-feeling is that of one body; when any limb of it aches, the whole body aches, because of sleeplessness and fever.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares believers to one body that reacts as a whole when any part is hurt.
islam.tie_back: Both texts use the body’s instinctive response to describe how friends respond to each other’s pain without stopping to think.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on the one-body image; the hadith stresses shared pain more than swift rescue.

judaism.quote_or_event: As soon as Abram hears that his kinsman Lot has been taken captive, he arms his 318 trained men, pursues the raiding kings through the night as far as Dan, and brings Lot back.
judaism.explanation: Abram acts the moment the news reaches him, without waiting or being asked.
judaism.tie_back: Abram’s instant rescue is the hand flying to the slipping garment.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on immediate rescue; Lot is a kinsman rather than a friend.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should a helpmate be understood as a warm-hearted friend: (i) he guards the heedless, (ii) he protects the wealth of the heedless, (iii) he becomes a refuge when you are in danger”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the true friend as one who protects you when you are off guard and becomes your refuge in danger.
buddhism.tie_back: Guarding the heedless is just what the hand does for the man who does not notice his garment slipping.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on protecting the off-guard friend; it lacks the Kural’s emphasis on speed.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Heracles goes down to Hades, he finds his friend Theseus held fast to the Chair of Forgetfulness and, taking him by the hand, pulls him free and brings him back to the living.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles takes the chance to free his friend the moment he finds him trapped.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The rescuing hand of Heracles is the Kural’s hand reaching out to remove a friend’s distress.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Fits immediate rescue by a friend’s hand; the Kural’s reflex-and-body image is absent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods … Or how can prosperity be guarded and preserved without friends? The greater it is, the more exposed is it to risk.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle opens his discussion of friendship by saying no one would choose life without friends, since friends are what guard us in fortune and in danger.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle sees friends as the protection that keeps a life from coming apart, the role the hand plays in the Kural.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Partial match on friends as protectors; Aristotle has nothing of the Kural’s instant, reflex-like help.

kurals.tamil:
நட்பிற்கு வீற்றிருக்கை யாதெனின் கொட்பின்றி
ஒல்லும்வாய் ஊன்றும் நிலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Natpirku veetrirukkai yaadhenin kotpindri
ollumvaai oondrum nilai.
kurals.meaning: If you ask where friendship sits enthroned, it is in the steady readiness, without wavering, to hold a friend up in every way one can.
kurals.elementary: Think of a walking stick that an old person leans on. It doesn’t move around or give up; it’s always there to take their weight. Valluvar says the very best friendship is like that stick: steady, never changing its mind, and always ready to hold you up however it can.
kurals.university: VīRRirukkai (வீற்றிருக்கை) means a throne or seat of majesty, so the question is ‘where is friendship’s throne?’, that is, what is its highest state. The answer has three parts: kotpu inRi (கொட்பின்றி, ‘without kotpu’, a word meaning whirling or wavering, so ‘without change of heart’); ollum vāy (ஒல்லும்வாய், ‘wherever and however possible’); and ūnRum nilai (ஊன்றும் நிலை, ‘the state of propping up, supporting’, as a staff supports). Parimelazhagar explains ollumvāy as helping in every way available toward the friend’s virtue and wealth, and kotpinri as never wavering in mind, whatever the times. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah gloss kotpinri as ‘always, without change’. Both web sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As a father tolerates the impudence of his son, a friend the impertinence of a friend, or a husband the familiarity of his wife, please tolerate the wrongs I may have done You.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna asks Krishna for the patient, unwavering forbearance that a friend shows toward a friend.
hinduism.tie_back: The friend’s steady tolerance is the Kural’s kotpinri, a support that does not waver or change its mind.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 11.44 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the constancy of friendship; the verse is about forbearance rather than active support.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus calls giving one’s life for one’s friends the greatest love.
christianity.tie_back: Laying down one’s life is the furthest limit of the Kural’s support ‘in every way one can’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the fullness of support; the Kural speaks of steady daily help rather than a single great sacrifice.

islam.quote_or_event: When the Emigrants arrived in Medina, the Prophet paired each with a Helper as a brother; the Helper Sa‘d ibn al-Rabi‘ offered to share half of all his property with ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf, who thanked him and asked only to be shown the market.
islam.explanation: The Helpers supported newly arrived strangers with everything they had, steadily and without being asked.
islam.tie_back: Sa‘d’s offer is the Kural’s ‘holding up in every way one can’, offered as a settled commitment.
islam._accuracy_note: Good illustration of total support; it is a story of a single generous offer rather than a statement of constancy.

judaism.quote_or_event: Though his father Saul is trying to kill David, Jonathan keeps faith with his friend, warns him of the danger, renews their covenant, and sends him away safely with the signal of the arrows.
judaism.explanation: Jonathan supports David at great cost to his own position as heir.
judaism.tie_back: Jonathan’s loyalty does not waver even under pressure from his own father, and he helps by every means he can.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on unwavering, active support.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who is the same in happiness and sorrow be understood as a warm-hearted friend: (i) he reveals his secrets, (ii) he conceals one’s own secrets, (iii) in misfortune he does not forsake one, (iv) his life even he sacrifices for one’s sake.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the friend who stays the same in good times and bad, even to the point of giving his life.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘The same in happiness and sorrow’ is the Kural’s kotpinri, friendship without wavering.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on unchanging support in all conditions.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the tyrant Dionysius condemned the Pythagorean Phintias (Pythias) to death, Damon stood surety for his life so that Phintias could settle his affairs; Phintias returned on the appointed day, and the tyrant, amazed, asked to be admitted as a third friend.
greek_mythology.explanation: Damon offered his own life as a pledge, and Phintias kept faith by returning to die.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s enthroned friendship: support given without hesitation and kept without wavering.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of steady loyalty; it is a legend of the Pythagoreans rather than of the gods and heroes.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “there is nothing which so fits in with our nature, or is so exactly what we want in prosperity or adversity.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius says friendship suits human nature better than anything else and is what we need in both good times and bad.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero’s friendship for ‘prosperity or adversity’ is the Kural’s support that holds steady in all seasons.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 5 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches friendship valid in all conditions; it lacks the Kural’s idea of steady propping-up.

kurals.tamil:
இனையர் இவரெமக்கு இன்னம்யாம் என்று
புனையினும் புல்லென்னும் நட்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Inaiyar ivaremakku innamyaam endru
punaiyinum pullennum natpu.
kurals.meaning: When friends go around saying, ‘He is this much to me, and I am that much to him,’ the friendship, however finely praised, becomes cheap.
kurals.elementary: Imagine two kids who keep telling everyone, ‘I’m her best friend, and I gave her THREE presents, and she’s SO lucky to have me!’ It starts to sound like showing off, and the friendship feels less special. Real friends don’t keep score or brag about it; they just are friends.
kurals.university: Inaiyar (இனையர்) means ‘such-and-such persons’ and innam (இன்னம்) ‘such-and-such’; the friend who says ‘he is so much to us, we are so much to him’ is measuring and advertising the friendship. Punaiyinum (புனையினும், ‘even if one adorns or praises it’) and pullennum (புல்லென்னும், ‘it looks mean or paltry’, from pul, grass, a common figure for worthlessness) complete the thought. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as a warning that true friends do not set their mutual services side by side or display their closeness, because keeping such accounts belongs to traders, not friends. The chapter thus ends where it began, by setting real friendship above any outward show. Both web sources give the same text; இவரெமக்கு is இவர் எமக்கு joined by sandhi.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Sudama, Krishna’s poor boyhood friend, visits him at Dwaraka, he is too shy to ask for anything and offers only a handful of flattened rice; Krishna receives him with great love, mentions no favour, and Sudama returns home to find his hut quietly turned into a palace.
hinduism.explanation: Neither friend counts or announces what the other means to him: Sudama asks for nothing, and Krishna gives without a word.
hinduism.tie_back: Their unspoken, unmeasured friendship is the opposite of the boasting the Kural warns against.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good positive counterpart to the Kural’s warning; the Purana does not itself criticise boastful friendship.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that blesseth his friend with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says loud, showy praise of a friend backfires and is taken as a curse.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point exactly: advertising a friendship cheapens it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close match on loud praise spoiling friendship.

islam.quote_or_event: “A man praised another man in front of the Prophet. The Prophet said to him, ‘Woe to you, you have cut off your companion’s neck, you have cut off your companion’s neck,’ repeating it several times”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that lavish praise of a companion harms him, and that such praise should be cautious and modest.
islam.tie_back: Both texts teach that over-praising a friend does damage rather than honour.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on the harm of extravagant praise; the hadith stresses spiritual harm to the one praised.

judaism.quote_or_event: Shammai teaches that one should say little and do much, and receive everyone with a cheerful face.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah prefers quiet deeds to many words.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s true friendship is likewise shown in deeds rather than declared in words.
judaism._accuracy_note: General ethical parallel on deeds over words; not specifically about friendship.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who renders lip-service be understood as a foe in the guise of a friend: (i) he makes friendly profession as regards the past, (ii) he makes friendly profession as regards the future, (iii) he tries to gain one’s favor by empty words, (iv) when opportunity for service has arisen, he expresses his inability.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha calls the person who keeps declaring friendship, past and future, but fails when needed, a foe dressed as a friend.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s talking-up of friendship, shown to be hollow.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on professed friendship being empty; the Sutta adds the failure to help.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Homer never has Achilles and Patroclus boast of what they are to each other; their bond shows in deeds, as when Patroclus puts on Achilles’ armour to save the Greeks, and Achilles speaks of it only in grief, after Patroclus is dead.
greek_mythology.explanation: The greatest friendship in Greek epic is told almost entirely through action, not through declarations.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ideal: a friendship that needs no announcing.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Interpretive parallel; the Iliad does not itself make the Kural’s point about boasting.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “there can be nothing more utterly subversive of friendship than flattery, adulation, and base compliance.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius names flattery and empty praise as the greatest destroyers of friendship.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero agrees with the Kural that the decorated words of friends cheapen what they praise.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 25 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good match on empty praise harming friendship; Cicero aims at flattery rather than self-advertisement.
